objectives: Explain why files are compressed and compare lossy with lossless compression for given scenarios.
Encode and decode data using run length encoding and dictionary coding, and evaluate the saving.
Compare symmetric and asymmetric encryption, including keys, speed and the key distribution problem.
Describe the properties of hashing and justify its use for passwords and fast lookup.

retrieval.q: An LMC program runs LDA NUM, ADD NUM, OUT, HLT with NUM DAT 6. What is output?
retrieval.a: 12: LDA loads 6 into the accumulator, ADD NUM adds 6 giving 12, OUT prints it (1.2.4).

retrieval.q: What is the difference between immediate and direct addressing?
retrieval.a: Immediate uses the operand itself as the value; direct treats the operand as the address of the value, one lookup (1.2.4).

retrieval.q: Under indirect addressing, what does the operand hold?
retrieval.a: The address of a location that holds the address of the value, so two lookups; it implements pointers (1.2.4).
Bundling data with its methods and making attributes private so they are accessed only through public methods (1.2.4).

retrieval.q: What is the difference between a class and an object?
retrieval.a: A class is the template or blueprint; an object is an instance of it created by instantiation (1.2.4).

keywords.def: Reduces file size with no permanent data loss; the exact original can be recovered.
Permanently removes data to shrink files much further; the original cannot be recovered.
Lossless technique replacing runs of repeated values with one value and a count.
Lossless technique storing repeated patterns once in a dictionary and replacing each with a short reference.
The same shared key both encrypts and decrypts; fast but the key must be exchanged securely.
A public and private key pair; data encrypted with one key is decrypted only by the other.
A hash of a message encrypted with the sender's private key, proving origin and integrity.
A one-way function turning an input into a fixed-length digest that cannot be reversed.
Two different inputs producing the same hash value; good hash functions make this rare.

content.heading: Why compress data
points: Compression reduces the number of bits needed to represent a file.
Smaller files need less storage space.
They transfer faster and use less bandwidth, so downloads and streaming work on slower connections.
The trade-off is processing time to compress and decompress.

content.heading: Lossless compression
points: No data is permanently removed: decompression rebuilds the exact original file.
Works by re-encoding redundancy, such as repeated values or patterns.
Essential for text, program code, spreadsheets and archives, where any change corrupts the file.
Examples: ZIP archives and PNG images; RLE and dictionary coding are lossless techniques.

content.heading: Lossy compression
points: Permanently removes data the human eye or ear barely notices.
Achieves much bigger savings than lossless, at the cost of some quality.
The original can never be recovered from the compressed file.
Examples: JPEG images, MP3 audio and streamed video.
Choose by scenario: photos for a web page tolerate loss; source code never does.

content.heading: Run length encoding
points: RLE replaces each run of identical values with the value and a count.
AAAABBB becomes 4A 3B: two pairs instead of seven characters.
It is lossless: expanding the counts rebuilds the data exactly.
Best on data with long runs, such as simple graphics with blocks of identical pixels.

content.heading: When RLE fails
points: With few or short runs there is nothing to shorten.
ABABAB becomes 1A 1B 1A 1B 1A 1B: six characters have become twelve.
Alternating or highly varied data can double in size under RLE.
Always state in answers that RLE only helps when long runs exist.
content.note: RLE does not always make a file smaller: a favourite examiner follow-up.

content.heading: Dictionary coding
points: Recurring patterns or words are stored once in a dictionary.
Each occurrence in the data is replaced by a short reference to its dictionary entry.
The dictionary must be stored or sent with the compressed file.
Lossless: substituting entries back for references rebuilds the original exactly.
Suits text, where the same words repeat; LZW and ZIP use dictionary methods.

content.heading: Symmetric encryption
points: Encryption scrambles plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and a key.
Symmetric encryption uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt.
It is fast, so it suits bulk data.
Weakness: both parties need the key, and sending it risks interception, the key distribution problem.

content.heading: Asymmetric encryption
points: Each user has a key pair: a public key shared openly and a private key kept secret.
A message encrypted with the recipient's public key can only be decrypted with their private key.
Anyone may encrypt to you, but only you can decrypt: distribution is solved.
It is slower than symmetric encryption, so it is used sparingly.

content.heading: Digital signatures and hybrid systems
points: To sign, the sender hashes the message and encrypts the hash with their private key.
The receiver decrypts the hash with the sender's public key, rehashes the message and compares.
A match proves who sent it and that it was not altered.
HTTPS uses asymmetric encryption to exchange a symmetric session key, then symmetric for the bulk data.

content.heading: Hashing and its uses
points: A hash function turns an input into a fixed-length digest.
It is one-way: the input cannot be recovered from the hash.
It is deterministic, fast, and good functions make collisions rare.
Passwords are stored as hashes; at login the entered password is hashed and the hashes compared.
Hash tables use the hash of a key as an address, giving near constant time lookup.
content.note: Hashing is not encryption: there is no key and no way back.

worked_examples.title: Run length encoding AAAABBBCCDAA
steps: Scan for runs: AAAA is 4 As, BBB is 3 Bs, CC is 2 Cs, D is 1 D, AA is 2 As.
Check the counts cover the original: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 12 characters, matching the input length.
Encode each run as count then value: 4A 3B 2C 1D 2A.
Compressed size: 5 pairs of two characters each = 10 characters, against 12 originally.
Saving: 2 characters, one sixth of the file; modest because two runs had length 1 and 2.
Contrast: ABABAB would encode as 1A 1B 1A 1B 1A 1B, growing from 6 to 12 characters.

worked_examples.title: Dictionary coding the cat and the dog and the rat
steps: Original text: the cat and the dog and the rat, which is 24 letters plus 7 spaces = 31 characters.
Build the dictionary of distinct words: 1 = the, 2 = cat, 3 = and, 4 = dog, 5 = rat.
Replace each word with its reference: the token stream is 1 2 3 1 4 3 1 5.
Check by decoding: the, cat, and, the, dog, and, the, rat matches the original exactly.
Assuming one character per token, the stream is 8 characters, but the 5-entry dictionary must also be stored.
Conclusion: overhead makes savings small on tiny files, but references pay off as repeated words multiply.

worked_examples.title: Asymmetric encryption and a digital signature between Alia and Ben
steps: Alia wants to send Ben a confidential contract that Ben can trust came from her.
Confidentiality: Alia encrypts the contract with Ben's public key, which anyone may hold.
Only Ben's private key can decrypt it, so interceptors see only ciphertext.
Signature: Alia hashes the contract and encrypts that hash with her own private key, attaching the result.
Ben decrypts the signature with Alia's public key, rehashes the received contract and compares the two hashes.
Matching hashes prove the message came from Alia's private key and was not altered in transit.

activities.title: Human run length encoding
instructions: Line up 17 students as a row of pixels: 6 holding A, then 3 holding B, then 8 holding C.
Ask how to describe the row to someone next door in the fewest characters; steer suggestions to RLE.
One student walks the line calling the encoding while a scribe writes it: A6 B3 C8, 17 characters described in 6.
Rearrange the same students into A B C A B C repeating and encode again.
Debrief: when does RLE shrink data and when does it inflate it?
activities.stretch: Encode the alternating row with dictionary coding instead, storing the pattern ABC once and referencing it, and compare which technique wins on each row.

activities.title: Padlocks and Caesar wheels: symmetric vs asymmetric
instructions: Symmetric round: Alia and Ben share the key shift plus 3; Alia encrypts REVISE to UHYLVH on a whiteboard and passes it through interceptor students, and Ben shifts back to decrypt.
Ask the interceptors what they saw, then the killer question: how could Alia and Ben have agreed the key without the interceptors hearing? Name the key distribution problem.
Asymmetric round: Ben hands out open padlocked boxes labelled his public key but keeps the only key in his pocket; Alia locks her message in a box and sends it through the same interceptors.
Debrief: same key both ways is symmetric, fast but with the distribution problem; public key locks and private key unlocks is asymmetric, slower but distribution is solved.
Finish by explaining HTTPS: asymmetric encryption shares a symmetric session key, then symmetric handles the bulk data for speed.
activities.stretch: Ask how Ben could prove a message really came from him: sign with his private key so anyone can verify with his public key, a digital signature.

activities.title: One-way street: human hash function
instructions: Define a toy hash on the board: hash(word) = number of letters MOD 5.
Students hash their own first name on mini-whiteboards and hold up the digit.
Ask: I am thinking of a word whose hash is 1; what was my word? Impossible: hashing is one-way.
Find two students with the same hash but different names and name it a collision.
Debrief which properties of a good hash the toy has, deterministic, fixed output, fast, and which it lacks, far too many collisions; link to password storage and hash tables.
activities.stretch: Ask why systems hash passwords rather than encrypting them: there is no key to steal and even an administrator with the database cannot reverse the hashes.

practice.q: A pixel row reads WWWWWBBWWWWWW. Show the result of run length encoding it and state the saving. (3)
practice.a: Runs are 5 W, 2 B, 6 W (1); encoded as 5W 2B 6W (1); 6 characters instead of 13, saving 7 characters (1).

practice.q: Explain why run length encoding could increase the size of some files. (2)
practice.a: RLE stores a count and value for every run (1); if runs are mostly length one, each single character becomes a two-character pair, up to doubling the file (1).

practice.q: A photographer emails proof images to clients, and a developer backs up source code. Justify a suitable compression type for each. (4)
practice.a: Photos: lossy (1), because large savings speed the email and small quality losses are invisible to clients (1). Source code: lossless (1), because every character must be recovered exactly or the program will not run (1).

practice.q: Describe how dictionary coding compresses a text file. (3)
practice.a: Repeated words or patterns are stored once in a dictionary (1); each occurrence is replaced by a short reference to its entry (1); the dictionary is stored with the file so decompression can substitute entries back exactly (1).

Symmetric uses one shared key for encryption and decryption; asymmetric uses a public and private key pair (1). Symmetric is faster and suits bulk data (1) but the shared key must be exchanged securely, the key distribution problem (1); asymmetric solves distribution because the public key is shared openly, though it is slower (1).

practice.q: Ben receives a message with a digital signature. Explain how he verifies who sent it and that it is unchanged. (3)
practice.a: He decrypts the signature with the sender's public key to recover the original hash (1); he hashes the received message himself (1); matching hashes prove the sender's private key signed it and the content was not altered (1).

practice.q: Explain why an online store should hash rather than encrypt its customers' passwords. (3)
practice.a: Hashing is one-way, so the password cannot be recovered even if the database is stolen (1); encryption is reversible, so a stolen key would expose every password (1); logins still work by hashing the entered password and comparing hashes (1).

practice.q: State two properties of a good hash function. (2)
practice.a: Any two of: one-way, so the input cannot be recovered (1); deterministic, with the same input always giving the same hash (1); quick to compute, or a low chance of collisions (1).

misconceptions: Students often think hashed data can be decrypted with the right key, but hashing is one-way and has no key at all.
Students often think lossy just means lower quality, but the defining point is that removed data can never be recovered.
Students often think RLE always shrinks files, but data without long runs can grow, even double.
Students often think the private key is shared between both parties, but only the public key is distributed; the private key never leaves its owner.
Students often think lossless means no compression happened, but it re-encodes redundancy while keeping the original exactly recoverable.
exam_link: Command words: state and describe for definitions and techniques, 2 to 3 marks; explain, compare and justify for scenarios, 3 to 4 marks.
Compression questions often supply raw data to encode with RLE, or a scenario asking you to choose and justify lossy or lossless.
Encryption questions reward precise key language: who holds which key, and which key performs each operation.
Example stem: A company sends confidential designs to a partner over the internet. Explain how asymmetric encryption keeps the designs secure. (4)
task: Produce a one-page comparison chart of RLE, dictionary coding, symmetric encryption, asymmetric encryption and hashing: what each does, whether it is reversible, one strength, one weakness and one real use.
challenge: A hospital must transmit patient scan images quickly to consultants and store staff passwords safely. Recommend and justify a compression choice for the scans, discussing the danger of lossy artefacts in diagnosis, then design the full login storage scheme naming where hashing is used and why encryption alone would be worse.

exit_ticket.q: Encode BBBBBBWWB with run length encoding.
exit_ticket.a: 6B 2W 1B: runs of 6, 2 and 1 covering all 9 characters.

exit_ticket.q: Which key does Alia use so only Ben can read her message, and which key opens it?
exit_ticket.a: She encrypts with Ben's public key; only Ben's private key can decrypt it.

exit_ticket.q: Give two reasons hashing suits password storage.
exit_ticket.a: It is one-way, so stored hashes cannot be turned back into passwords; login comparison still works by hashing the attempt and comparing digests.
